_note: DATA-extra: county-, city-, water-management-district- and privately-run Florida swim spots that are not state parks. Same ParkSeed shape as data/parks.deep.json. nws_grid / nws_zone / nws_county are deliberately null - the alerts cron fills them. Every non-obvious fact has a URL in sources[].

parks.name: Hart Springs Park
parks.hours: April 1 - September 30: 9 a.m. to 7:30 p.m. daily. October 1 - March 31: 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. daily.
parks.fees: April - September: $5 per person Monday-Friday, $8 per person Saturday, Sunday and holidays. October - March: $3 per person. Children 5 and under and seniors 65 and over are free. Camping and the Hart Springs House are booked separately through ReserveAmerica.

rules.alcohol: No alcohol anywhere in the park, and intoxicated people are not admitted.
rules.tubing: Not a tubing run - the spring run is short and empties into the Suwannee River. No published tube rental or float trip.
rules.pets: No pets in the day-use springs area. Pets are allowed in the RV park and on the nature trails only, under the park's pet policy.
rules.life_jackets: No published restriction on life jackets or personal flotation devices in the swimming area.
other: No glass in common areas or in the springs.
No fishing in the swimming area.
Smoking and vaping are prohibited throughout the park, including the parking lots and the boardwalk.
Noise and music must stay in the vicinity of your shelter or picnic area.
No generators in the day-use area.

parks.safety_notes: No lifeguards on duty - swim at your own risk. The spring stays about 72 F year round, cold enough to tire swimmers quickly. The spring run flows into the Suwannee River; when the river is high it backs into the spring pool and the water turns dark and loses visibility. Alligators and water snakes live in the river and can move into the run. The boardwalk and steps get slippery.
parks.entrance_notes: Gilchrist County park at 4240 SW 86th Avenue, Bell. One gated day-use entrance with a staffed booth; the campground entrance is separate at 4183 SW 80th Ct. The park sets a daily capacity: once capacity is reached only people who already hold a wristband or have a shelter/pavilion reservation are let in, so a reserved shelter or Pavilion A or B guarantees your group entry on a busy day. Pay per person, not per car.
parks.description: A Gilchrist County park on the Suwannee River with one of the largest spring-fed swimming areas in Florida, plus a half-mile boardwalk along the spring run. It is a pay-per-person day-use park that stops admitting new visitors once it hits its daily capacity.

parks.name: Lithia Springs Conservation Park
parks.hours: 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. daily in spring and summer; 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. in fall and winter. The swimming area closes one hour before the park closes. Swimming runs in two four-hour slots: 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. and 2 p.m. to 6 p.m.
parks.fees: $2 per vehicle to enter (up to 8 people per vehicle) plus $2 per person to swim. Camping is charged separately.

rules.alcohol: Hillsborough County does not publish an alcohol rule for the Lithia Springs swim area; assume alcohol is not permitted in the spring and check at the gate.
rules.tubing: Not a tubing run. Round rings and inflatable toys are allowed in the shallow areas only.
rules.pets: Pets and service animals are not permitted inside the spring area. Elsewhere in the county park pets must be on a hand-held leash and picked up after.
rules.life_jackets: Arm floaties and life vests are allowed in all parts of the spring. No flotation devices in the deep end.
other: Swim bands are sold at the gate only - they cannot be reserved ahead or bought over the phone, and there are no rain checks or refunds.
Each four-hour swim slot is capped at 200 swimmers.
No Bluetooth speakers in the swimming area.
No hammocks or anything attached to trees or the fence inside the swimming area.
No bounce houses in the park.
A responsible adult over 18 must supervise children under 12.
Swim bands are not sold in the hour before the swimming area closes.
Bands are sold only to people already at the park, and only for one of the two slots.
The swim area is sanitised between the two slots.
The swimming area closes for thunder, lightning and inclement weather.
Picnic shelters are not rented April-September; shelters, tables, grills and parking spaces are first come, first served.

parks.safety_notes: Hillsborough County does not publish lifeguard coverage for the spring - plan on swimming at your own risk. The spring holds about 72 F year round and has a roped deep end where no flotation devices are allowed. The spring run empties into the Alafia River a short walk away; after heavy rain the river rises, the water turns murky and the county closes the spring for swimming. Alligators live in the Alafia River system.
parks.entrance_notes: Hillsborough County park at 3932 Lithia Springs Rd., Lithia. One entrance station: you pay the $2 vehicle fee there and buy $2 swim bands for anyone going in the spring. Bands are sold in person only, for one of the two four-hour slots, and each slot is capped at 200 swimmers, so weekends and holidays sell out - arrive at the start of the slot. The park itself, the campground and the trails stay open even when the spring is closed.
parks.description: A Hillsborough County conservation park east of Tampa built around a clear, second-magnitude spring with a fenced swimming area and a campground. Swimming is sold in two capacity-limited four-hour sessions, so on hot weekends the bands run out well before the slot ends.

parks.name: Hunter Springs Park
parks.hours: 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. from April 1 (or the first day of daylight saving time, whichever comes first) through Labor Day; 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. from the day after Labor Day through October 31; 8 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. from November 1 (or the day after daylight saving ends, whichever is later) through March 31. Restrooms close 30 minutes before the park.
parks.fees: Paid parking and a separate per-vessel paddle-craft launch fee, both collected at the pay station. Credit or debit card only - have your vehicle tag number ready. City of Crystal River resident annual parking passes are accepted in place of the parking fee; commercial and county launch passes are not valid here. The city does not publish the dollar amount online; third-party guides report about $5 to park and $5 per paddle-craft launch.

rules.alcohol: No alcoholic beverages and no glass containers anywhere in the park.
rules.tubing: No tubing run. The swimming area is a roped-off freshwater beach on Kings Bay; the city rents no paddle-craft and commercial launching is not allowed.
rules.pets: No dogs or pets in the park. Service animals are permitted under Titles II and III of the ADA.
rules.life_jackets: No published restriction on life jackets in the roped swim area.
other: No jumping, diving or climbing from or on the boardwalk.
No fishing anywhere in the park or from the shoreline.
No tents, canopies or umbrellas over 4 feet across.
No loud sound-making devices; no smoking except in designated areas.
No oversized vehicle or trailer parking, and no overnight parking - cars left at closing may be towed.
Children 12 and under may not be left unattended.
Do not feed or disturb the manatees and other wildlife.

parks.safety_notes: No lifeguards - swim at your own risk. The spring vent sits about 100 feet offshore and keeps the water near 72 F year round. This is open water on Kings Bay: boat traffic runs just outside the swim buoys, manatees are present (especially November to March) and must not be touched or chased, and alligators occasionally enter the bay. The bottom drops off and visibility falls after wind or heavy rain.
parks.entrance_notes: City of Crystal River park at 104 NE 1st Ave, a residential street corner with a small paid lot - no oversized vehicles or trailers. Pay at the station by card with your tag number before you walk in. The lot is the limiting factor on manatee-season weekends; overflow parking in the neighbourhood is restricted and cars left at closing are towed.
parks.description: A small city park on Kings Bay in Crystal River with a sandy freshwater beach, a roped swim area fed by an offshore spring vent, a kayak launch and a manatee-viewing boardwalk. The water stays about 72 F all year, which is why manatees crowd in during cold months.

parks.name: Little River Springs Park
parks.hours: April - October: 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. November - March: 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Open year round.

rules.tubing: No tubing run. The spring run is only about 150 feet long before it reaches the Suwannee River.
rules.life_jackets: No published restriction on life jackets in the spring.
other: Open water swimming and snorkelling in the spring pool and run; picnic pavilions and portable restrooms on site.
The underwater cave is for cave-certified divers only - open-water divers and snorkellers must stay out of the cave.

parks.safety_notes: No published lifeguard coverage - swim at your own risk. The water is about 72 F year round and the spring pool drops off steeply to the cave entrance. More than 1,200 feet of underwater cave runs back from the vent and it is a well-known cave-diving site: entering it without cave certification, lights and a guideline is how divers die here. The run empties into the Suwannee River, so when the river is high it pushes tannic water back into the pool and visibility disappears. Alligators use the river.
parks.entrance_notes: Suwannee County park at 24891 105th Ln., O'Brien, about 3 miles north of Branford. One gated entrance with a $5 per-vehicle honour/attendant fee - this fee only started recently, so older guides that call it free are out of date. Paved parking, paved walkways and three accessible pavilions; restrooms are portable units. Divers and swimmers share the same small pool.
parks.description: A 125-acre Suwannee County park on the Suwannee River, built around a clear spring pool that stays near 72 F all year. It is popular with swimmers and snorkellers and is also the entrance to a long underwater cave system that draws cave divers from around the world.

parks.name: Royal Springs Park
parks.hours: April - October: 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. November - March: 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Open year round.

rules.tubing: No tubing run. The spring boil sits beside the Suwannee River with a short run.
rules.life_jackets: No published restriction on life jackets in the spring.
other: Two sets of stairs lead into the water and there is a jumping/diving platform over the boil.
A one-lane concrete boat ramp gives access to the Suwannee River - keep clear of the ramp when swimming.
Restrooms on site are portable units.

parks.safety_notes: No published lifeguard coverage - swim at your own risk. The spring stays about 72 F year round, cold enough to tire swimmers quickly, and the boil is deep right under the jumping platform - check the depth and clear the water below before anyone jumps. The stairs and platform get slippery. The spring sits next to the Suwannee River and a boat ramp; when the river runs high it floods the boil with dark water and swimming is not worth it. Alligators use the river.
parks.entrance_notes: Suwannee County park at 20091 157th Ln., O'Brien, in a rural stretch south of Live Oak. One entrance with a $5 per-vehicle fee. The lot also serves the boat ramp, so it fills with trailers on good river days. Facilities are basic: one picnic pavilion, tables and grills, and portable toilets.
parks.description: A small Suwannee County park on the Suwannee River whose large spring boil is popular with swimmers, snorkellers and jumpers from the platform above it. Stairs lead into the water and a one-lane ramp next door launches boats onto the river.

parks.name: Suwannee Springs
parks.hours: Daylight hours only: 1.5 hours before sunrise to 1.5 hours after sunset, unless otherwise posted. No overnight parking.
parks.fees: Free - no entrance or parking fee on Suwannee River Water Management District lands.

rules.alcohol: Alcoholic beverages, intoxicants and illegal drugs are prohibited on District lands.
rules.tubing: No organised tubing run. People float and swim in the river and off the white sand bars beside the spring house.
rules.pets: Dogs are allowed but must be on a leash.
rules.life_jackets: No published restriction on life jackets; the Suwannee River here has current, so wear one if you are not a strong swimmer.
other: Scuba diving is prohibited on District lands.
No fires of any kind.
Camping only by special use authorisation - this is a day-use site.
Do not remove plants, animals or anything from the historic 1800s spring house.

parks.safety_notes: No lifeguards and no staff on site - the District states plainly that it gives no assurance the area is safe. This is a sulphur spring inside a roofless 1800s limestone spring house right on the bank of the Suwannee River: the water smells of sulphur, is about 72 F, and the walls are old, uneven and slick. The river itself has current and dark tannic water, and when it rises it floods the spring house completely and the swimming is gone until it drops. Alligators and water snakes use the river.
parks.entrance_notes: A 115-acre Suwannee River Water Management District tract (the District is a regional public agency, not a county - LakeLens files public non-state sites like this under 'county'). From US 129 north of Live Oak turn onto 93rd Drive (Old US 129), go north to 32nd Street and turn right to the parking lot. Unstaffed and free; facilities are a picnic area, restrooms and a canoe launch. Check the Suwannee River gauge at Suwannee Springs (USGS 02315550, essentially on site) before you drive out - a high river means the spring house is under water.
parks.description: A free, unstaffed water-management-district tract on the Suwannee River where a sulphur spring bubbles up inside the stone walls of an 1800s spring house. People swim in the spring house and off the white sand bars along the river beside it.

parks.name: Otter Springs Park & Campground
parks.hours: Gilchrist County does not publish day-use hours online. Call the park at (352) 463-0800 before you go.
parks.fees: Gilchrist County does not publish a day-use fee online; an entry fee is charged. Campsites and cabins are booked through ReserveAmerica. Call (352) 463-0800 to confirm.

rules.alcohol: No alcohol rule is published for the day-use area; Gilchrist County's other spring park (Hart Springs) bans alcohol outright, so expect the same and confirm at the gate.
rules.tubing: No tubing run. Swimming is in the spring in the picnic area or in the swimming pool, which is heated in winter.
rules.pets: No pet policy is published for the day-use area; confirm with the park.
rules.life_jackets: No published restriction on life jackets.
other: Two separate places to swim: the second-magnitude spring in the picnic area and a heated swimming pool.
Hiking trails run from the park down to the Suwannee River.
Basketball court and volleyball net on site.

parks.safety_notes: No published lifeguard coverage for the spring - swim at your own risk. The spring holds about 72 F year round. The spring run drains to the Suwannee River a short walk away, so a high river backs tannic water up into the spring and kills the clarity; the pool is the fallback on those days. Alligators use the river and the lower run.
parks.entrance_notes: Gilchrist County park at 6470 SW 80th Avenue, Trenton, just east of Fanning Springs. The county took management of the park back in-house on 16 February 2026 after it had been run under contract, and the park reopened on 1 May 2026, so hours, fees and rules published before 2026 are unreliable - phone (352) 463-0800 or the county at (352) 463-3444 to confirm before driving out.
parks.description: A 500-acre Gilchrist County park and campground near Fanning Springs with a second-magnitude spring in the picnic area and a separate heated swimming pool. Trails run from the campground down to the Suwannee River.

parks.name: Morrison Springs County Park
parks.hours: Open daily, sunrise to sunset. The park closes at dusk - there is no night diving, by Walton County ordinance 2007-09.
parks.fees: $4 per vehicle at the gate. Credit or debit card only - no cash is accepted. The fee started on 1 March 2026; guides written before then that call the park free are out of date.

rules.alcohol: Walton County does not publish an alcohol rule on the park page; third-party guides report alcohol and loud music are not allowed. Confirm at the entrance building.
rules.tubing: No tubing run. The spring pool drains through a short run to the Choctawhatchee River.
rules.pets: No pet policy is published on the county park page - confirm at the gate.
rules.life_jackets: No published restriction on life jackets in the spring pool.
other: No night diving (county ordinance 2007-09); the park closes at dusk.
No motorized boats upstream of the boat ramp toward the spring - kayaks and row boats only.
The boat ramp is more than 100 yards from the diving area, so boat traffic and divers stay separated.
Outdoor shower heads at the restrooms for swimmers and divers.

parks.safety_notes: No lifeguards - swim at your own risk. The spring pool is about 250 feet across and holds roughly 72 F water year round. Three cavern openings lead down from the pool and the deepest cavity reaches about 300 feet: the shallow openings are cavern dives, and the deep system is for cave-certified divers with proper gear only. Divers and swimmers share the same pool, so watch for bubbles and dive flags. When the Choctawhatchee River floods it backs tannic water into the spring and clarity disappears - Walton County publishes a 1-5 water clarity rating on the park page.
parks.entrance_notes: Walton County park at 874 Morrison Springs Road, Ponce de Leon - a 161-acre site off SR 81. Since March 2026 there is an entrance building with a card-only $4 per-vehicle gate; bring a card, not cash. Wheelchair-accessible boardwalks run to the diver's dock and to the beach area, with accessible parking near the pavilions. The boat ramp has its own separate parking lot.
parks.description: A Walton County park in the Florida Panhandle built around a wide, clear spring pool that pushes out roughly 48 million gallons a day. It is one of northwest Florida's best-known dive sites and also a straightforward place to swim from the beach and boardwalks.

parks.name: Vortex Spring Adventures
parks.hours: Monday to Thursday 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.; Friday to Sunday 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. (Central time). Open year round except Thanksgiving and Christmas. Quiet hours midnight to 8 a.m. in the campground.
parks.fees: Day use $15 for ages 13 and up, $10 for ages 12 and under, free under 4 (plus tax). Snorkel gear add-on $6. Daily diving pass $25. Camping, cabins and golf-cart rental are extra.

rules.alcohol: Personal alcohol is allowed for guests of legal age, but you may not sell or serve alcohol to other guests. Divers must never dive under the influence of alcohol or drugs.
rules.tubing: No tubing run. Swimming, snorkelling and diving are all in the spring basin and its short run.
rules.pets: Pets are allowed in designated campground areas only, on a leash no longer than 6 feet and cleaned up after. They are not allowed near the spring, swim areas, decks, docks, slides or platforms, or in lodging, retail or the restaurant. Service animals are allowed anywhere guests may go.
rules.life_jackets: No published restriction on life jackets. Everyone must sign a waiver before swimming - adults sign their own, a parent or guardian signs for minors.
other: Glass is prohibited everywhere in the spring and pool areas - drinks must be in cans or sealed plastic.
Divers must show certification; minimum diving age is 10 and minors must dive with a certified adult.
No cavern or cave entry without the matching certification.
Golf carts and ATVs need proof of liability insurance and a signed waiver.
Admission can be revoked without refund for breaking park rules.

parks.safety_notes: Privately run, with waivers instead of lifeguards - swim at your own risk. The basin holds about 68 F water year round, colder than most Florida springs, and it is deep. This is a cave system with a history: after a run of fatalities the operators installed a locked steel gate roughly 300 feet into the cave at about 110 feet deep, and only cave-certified divers get it opened, usually with a staff member. Open-water divers and snorkellers must stay out of the cave. Bubbles and dive flags are everywhere - swimmers should keep clear of the dive platforms.
parks.entrance_notes: Privately owned resort at 1517 Vortex Springs Lane, Ponce de Leon (Holmes County) - not a public park, so county and state park passes do not apply and admission is charged per person at the gate. Everyone signs a waiver before getting in the water. The dive shop handles diving check-in and rentals; call (850) 836-4979 to confirm trail and facility availability, which changes with weather and events.
parks.description: A privately run spring resort in the Panhandle with a walled swimming basin, dive platforms, a dive shop, campground and cabins. It is best known as a training site for divers, with a gated cave system that only cave-certified divers may enter.

parks.name: Williford Spring Recreation Area
parks.hours: 8 a.m. until sunset, seven days a week. Day use only.
parks.fees: Free - no entrance or parking fee.

rules.alcohol: Alcoholic beverages are prohibited throughout the Econfina Creek Water Management Area.
rules.tubing: Tubing on Econfina Creek runs from the Pitt and Sylvan Springs site downstream; Williford has a canoe/kayak launch at the end of the boardwalk, but no vessels are allowed in the spring itself.
rules.pets: No pet rule is published for this site; dogs are generally allowed on District lands under control.
rules.life_jackets: No published restriction on life jackets.
other: No vessels - canoes, kayaks, paddleboards - inside the spring area.
No ATVs anywhere in the water management area; motorized vehicles on designated roads only.
Three first-come picnic pavilions and two composting toilets; no drinking water.
A mile-long nature trail connects to Pitt and Sylvan Springs.

parks.safety_notes: No lifeguards and no staff on site - swim at your own risk. The spring runs about 72 F year round. Entry is by steps with handrails into a boil that is deeper than it looks; the boardwalk and steps are slick. The spring run joins Econfina Creek within a few hundred feet, and the creek has real current plus snags - after heavy rain it rises fast and turns dark. Alligators and water snakes use the creek. Only composting toilets and no drinking water, so bring your own.
parks.entrance_notes: A Northwest Florida Water Management District recreation site at 5647 Porter Pond Road, Youngstown, in Washington County (the District is a regional public land-management agency, not a county - LakeLens files public non-state sites like this under 'county'). From US 231 go about 7 miles west and turn north onto Porter Pond Road, roughly 1.5 miles north of SR 20. Free and unstaffed, with a boardwalk system around the spring, mobility access and steps with handrails into the water. The small gravel lot is the limit on summer weekends.
parks.description: A free water-management-district site on Econfina Creek in the Panhandle, with a boardwalk ringing a clear spring and handrailed steps down into the boil. A nature trail links it to the Pitt and Sylvan Springs site about a mile away.

parks.name: Pitt and Sylvan Springs Recreation Area
parks.hours: 8 a.m. until sunset, seven days a week. Day use only.
parks.fees: Free - no entrance or parking fee. Tube and shuttle rentals from private outfitters on SR 20 are separate.

rules.alcohol: Alcoholic beverages are prohibited throughout the Econfina Creek Water Management Area.
rules.tubing: Yes - this is the Econfina Creek tubing site. There is a tube put-in dock at the Sylvan Spring end and a take-out dock where the Pitt Spring run meets Econfina Creek.
rules.pets: No pet rule is published for this site; dogs are generally allowed on District lands under control.
rules.life_jackets: No published restriction on life jackets; Econfina Creek has current, so wear one if you are not a strong swimmer.
other: Day use only - no camping.
Swimming area has safety railings.
Canoe/kayak launch with a tie-up area for a quick stop.
Composting restrooms and first-come picnic pavilions; overflow parking is reached from Porter Pond Road.
No ATVs; motorized vehicles on designated roads only.

parks.safety_notes: No lifeguards and no staff on site - swim at your own risk. The springs run about 72 F. This is the busiest tubing put-in on Econfina Creek, so expect tube traffic in the run on summer weekends. The creek is not a lazy river: it has current, undercut banks, submerged logs and a few pinch points, and after heavy rain it rises fast and turns dark - check the Econfina Creek gauge near Bennett before floating. Alligators and water snakes use the creek. Composting toilets only and no drinking water.
parks.entrance_notes: A 10-acre Northwest Florida Water Management District site at 6315 E. Highway 20, Youngstown, in Bay County (the District is a regional public land-management agency, not a county - LakeLens files public non-state sites like this under 'county'). Free and unstaffed, right on SR 20. The main lot fills on summer weekends; overflow parking is off Porter Pond Road. A mile-long connector trail runs to Williford Spring.
parks.description: A free water-management-district site on Econfina Creek where Pitt and Sylvan springs feed a short clear run into the creek. It has railed swimming areas, boardwalks, and the put-in and take-out docks for the Econfina Creek tube float.

parks.name: Cypress Spring
parks.hours: Daylight hours. There is no gate and no staff - it is reached from the water on Holmes Creek.
parks.fees: Free to reach by your own boat. Private outfitters on Cypress Springs Road and at Holmes Creek landings charge for kayak, canoe and paddleboard rental and shuttles.

rules.alcohol: Alcoholic beverages are prohibited on Holmes Creek (Northwest Florida Water Management District rule).
rules.tubing: People float and paddle the Holmes Creek run past the spring; there is no formal tube launch at the spring itself.
rules.pets: No pet rule is published for this site; dogs are generally allowed on District lands under control.
rules.life_jackets: No published restriction, but this is a creek paddle - Florida law requires a wearable life jacket aboard for every person and children under 6 must wear one on a vessel under 26 feet.
other: No ATVs; motorized vehicles on designated roads only.
No facilities at the spring - no restrooms, no drinking water, no trash service. Pack it out.
Watch for the federally protected Gulf sturgeon, which congregate in the lower Choctawhatchee near the Holmes Creek confluence.

parks.safety_notes: No lifeguards, no staff and no phone signal to speak of - this is a remote, water-access spring. The boil is about 72 F and deep, with a cavern vent that divers enter; snorkellers and untrained divers must stay out of it. Holmes Creek has current and boat traffic, and when the Choctawhatchee system rises the creek floods the spring with dark water and the swimming is over until it drops - check the Holmes Creek gauge at Vernon first. Alligators and water snakes use the creek.
parks.entrance_notes: A first-magnitude spring on Holmes Creek in Washington County, protected by the Northwest Florida Water Management District with Washington County (the District is a regional public land-management agency, not a county - LakeLens files public non-state sites like this under 'county'). Note the spring is on Holmes Creek, not Econfina Creek. There is no road-side public park: the usual approach is a paddle from Cypress Springs Road or a Holmes Creek landing such as Cotton Landing. The District began a shoreline restoration project here on 8 January 2026 - shoreline access may still be restricted, but the spring stays reachable by watercraft.
parks.description: A big, clear first-magnitude spring on Holmes Creek in the Panhandle, reached by paddling rather than by driving to a car park. Swimmers and snorkellers float in the boil while the creek carries on past it.
